context: heavy foundations & crane structure · hot commissioning on live process media

brief.intro: New to this project type? A steel plant (steelworks) converts scrap or hot metal into finished steel through three linked stages: melting/refining in a furnace or converter, continuous casting into semi-finished shapes, and rolling into final product. Unlike a normal industrial building, the structure exists to carry molten metal safely — foundations for the furnace, caster and mill stands are enormous, and overhead cranes that move ladles of liquid steel must be operating before the process equipment inside them can even be set. Your schedule is won or lost on three things: sequencing crane readiness ahead of heavy internals, respecting the fixed-duration refractory dry-out cure, and proving the plant cold (mechanically) before it is proven hot (with real heat and metal).

scope.name: Structural steel & building envelope
scope.desc: Portal-frame melt-shop and mill bays, crane-rail-supporting columns, roofing/cladding.

scope.name: Melting & refining
scope.desc: Electric arc furnace (EAF) or basic oxygen furnace (BOF), ladle furnace, refractory lining and its dry-out/heat-up curing.

scope.name: Continuous casting
scope.desc: Caster machine, ladle turret, tundish car, mould and spray-cooling — casts liquid steel into billets, blooms or slabs.

scope.name: Rolling mill
scope.desc: Hot/cold mill stands, roll-line, coilers and shears — reduces cast product to final section or coil.

scope.name: Overhead cranes
scope.desc: Ladle and charging cranes on crane rails — must be commissioned ahead of the heavy internals they will install and later operate.

scope.name: Process media systems
scope.desc: Fuel gas, oxygen/nitrogen/argon, direct & indirect cooling water — live utilities the furnace and mill depend on.

scope.name: Electrical power & drives
scope.desc: MV substations, furnace/electrode transformers, large mill motor drives and VFDs.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Cold (mechanical) commissioning, refractory heat-up, then hot commissioning — first melt, first cast, first roll.

glossary.plain: electric arc furnace / basic oxygen furnace — the vessel that melts scrap or hot metal into liquid steel.
casts liquid steel into semi-finished shapes (billets, blooms or slabs) in one continuous strand.
refractory-lined vessels that carry and meter molten steel between the furnace and the caster.
heat-resistant brick or castable lining that protects steel vessels from molten metal — installed then cured (dried and heated) before use.
cold = proving the equipment mechanically with no heat or metal; hot = the real thing, with actual molten steel live.
the rolling equipment that reduces cast steel to its final rolled shape or coil.
the rails and structure supporting overhead cranes that handle ladles and coils above the process floor.
the fuel gas, oxygen, nitrogen/argon and cooling water that the furnace and mill consume while running.

must_get_right: Sequence overhead cranes and structural steel ahead of heavy-equipment set — the crane has to be operating before the furnace shell, ladle turret or mill stands it will install can go in.
Refractory dry-out/heat-up is a fixed-duration cure set by the refractory supplier's curve — build it into the critical path as real duration, never compress or resequence it.
Cold (mechanical) commissioning must be fully proven system-by-system before molten metal is introduced — treat the cold-to-hot gate as hard, not a formality.
Process media (fuel gas, oxygen, cooling water) must be live and proven before hot commissioning starts — it is a hard predecessor, not parallel scope.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Heavy-lift and crane-availability constraints are carried as activity codes rather than hard date constraints, so the network stays float-driven.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day single-shift week; equipment erection and media works move to two shifts where needed to protect the critical path. Refractory dry-out runs a continuous 24/7 calendar dictated by the refractory manufacturer's fixed heat-up curve — it cannot be compressed by adding resources. Hot commissioning runs 24/7 once initiated.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs heavy foundations → crane rails & structural steel → furnace/converter & caster erection → refractory installation & dry-out (fixed-duration cure) → process-media proving → cold commissioning → hot commissioning → production ramp-up. Overhead cranes are an early-network gate, not a late one: the crane must be operating before the furnace shell, ladle turret or mill stands it will install can go in.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and vendor drawings issued before foundation design is finalised; overhead cranes are commissioned ahead of heavy-internals installation; the refractory supplier's dry-out curve is followed exactly, never compressed; utility tie-ins (gas, power, water) are available by the media-proving milestone.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy lifts (furnace shell, caster segments, mill stands) need crane capacity and clear laydown before the permanent cranes are commissioned — a temporary heavy-lift crane is typically mobilised early. Refractory bricklayers and specialist mechanical-alignment crews are a constrained, specialist resource. Hot commissioning needs the full multi-discipline team on site simultaneously.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-lead equipment slippage, refractory dry-out schedule slip (curing issues can force a re-cure), and a failed first-melt/first-cast hot-commissioning attempt requiring rework before a second trial. Schedule contingency is held immediately before refractory dry-out start and before hot commissioning, not spread thinly across the network.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for equipment erection and refractory works — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
